einzeiler: Doug Leone on Sequoia, fear, great founders, and starting over at 69.
kurzfassung: Doug Leone reflects on his decades-long career at Sequoia Capital, discussing how fear and personal drive fuel his ambition. He shares lessons on partnering with extreme founders, the importance of trust, and his decision to return to the firm. Throughout the conversation, Leone emphasizes the value of long-term commitment and maintaining high standards in business.
stichpunkte: Leone views fear and insecurity as powerful motivators rather than obstacles, driving his desire to remain relevant.
He credits early hardships and working-class roots as the foundation for his unrelenting competitive drive.
Sequoia Capital's success is built on backing extreme outliers and uncompromising founders who obsess over their problems.
Trust is described as the critical accelerant for business, combining both technical competence and pure intentions.
Leone admits to the common venture capital mistake of selling winning investments too early.
He stresses the importance of deliberate board construction, treating board members like lifetime business partners.
Leone returned to Sequoia to help navigate the massive technological shifts brought by artificial intelligence.

clips.hook: Feeling inadequate after decades of success
clips.text: Following a brief break from work, the veteran investor admits feeling completely useless and threatened by recent technological advancements.

clips.hook: Testing personal toughness with a root canal
clips.text: To test his own mental fortitude, the speaker deliberately underwent a dental procedure without any local anesthesia.

clips.hook: Massive early stakes in legendary tech giants
clips.text: The firm secured remarkably high ownership percentages in some of the most dominant technology companies in history.
A massive portion of investors in the startup ecosystem lack genuine capability or actively damage the companies they join.
Meeting unfamiliar individuals initially brings a strong sense of dread rather than excitement for an introvert.

beschreibung:
Doug Leone spent 26 years helping lead Sequoia Capital through successive eras of technological change. Born in Italy, he came to the United States without speaking English and carried the insecurity of an outsider into his career. That fear became fuel: whenever he felt himself falling behind, he forced himself to start over. After stepping down from Sequoia at 65 to make room for the next generation, he returned four years later. Now he considers himself a low-level analyst again, racing to understand an AI revolution that he believes is rewriting business more radically than anything he has seen before.

Leone explains the three questions he asks before making an investment: Would he put his children's money into it? If he could make only 20 investments in his life, would this be one of them? Could it return the entire fund? He is interested only in extreme outliers—companies capable of returning 100 times the original investment—and says the biggest mistake venture investors make is selling their winners too early. Sequoia once owned enormous stakes in Apple, Cisco, Google and NVIDIA, but even the greatest investors failed to anticipate how long exceptional companies could continue compounding.

His role as an investor is not to shape a founder's technology. It is to help turn a product into a business: recruiting the first team, building sales and marketing, navigating crucible moments and preserving the founder as the soul of the company. He describes backing David Vélez before Nubank existed, what Fred Luddy's unusual ServiceNow pitch revealed about him and why Sequoia looks for the same qualities in founders and its own partners: a hypercompetitive person with a heart of gold.

Leone also discusses trust as the accelerant that makes business move quickly. Trust requires both competence and good intentions, and it is earned by helping founders when they are most vulnerable. He explains why founders should architect their boards as carefully as their products, why productive disagreement is different from argument and how to deliver difficult feedback so it can actually be heard. He closes with lessons from his longtime partner Michael Moritz: listen to the exact words people choose, put the other person first and always ask what a company could become if everything goes right.
